entries.name: openclaw 2026.8.34
entries.purpose: This is a gateway-only extended-stable release, which is our current equivalent to LTS. This release is OpenClaw from the end of August 2026, plus critical security updates, reliability and performance fixes, and features like new model support. The latest version of OpenClaw at the time of this release is 2026.9.7 2026.8.34 Highlights Extended-stable correctness rollup: backport 113 audit-selected fix units across upgrades, Doctor, authentication, sessions, channels, plugins, sandboxing, filesystem safety, model runtimes, and release packaging. Complete rescan: re-evaluate the full 2026.8.33 discovery range, large mixed-purpose pull requests, and the 2026.7.35 lineage instead of advancing only from the previous backport cursor. Upgrade and recovery hardening: preserve credentials, agent state, plugin inventory, transcripts, schedules, service ownership, and runtime links through upgrades, restarts, and Doctor repair. Boundary fixes: tighten remote filesystem mutation, plugin and skill scanning, browser authentication, channel reply identity, private skill ingress, and scoped runtime ownership. Changes Extended-stable release preparation: align OpenClaw, publishable plugins, native version metadata, generated channel catalogs, and npm package inventories to 2026.8.34. Fixes Plugins: Recover orphan installs without weakening ownership. Doctor: Repair keyed multi-agent rosters without ownership (#134706) Prevent device pairing migration crash on contaminated records. Doctor: Preserve per-agent memory search during upgrades. Doctor: Detect shared auth migration by provenance (#134808) Cron: Refuse stale doctor store rewrites. Gateway: Refresh model catalog after auth changes (#134361) Openai: Repair stale doctor route pins.

entries.name: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction
entries.purpose: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.

entries.name: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding
entries.purpose: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.

entries.name: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively
entries.purpose: Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success-failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents'robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex.

entries.name: REMORY: Learning Residual Memory for Context Compaction
entries.purpose: Long-horizon agents compact their history to continue within a finite context window, but a textual summary alone may not support every subsequent decision. We introduce REMORY, a neural memory network that supplements the summary with a bounded sequence of soft memory tokens. Given the history and summary, the network learns to generate tokens that help a frozen LLM approximate the continuation it would produce with the full history. The tokens are conditioned on the summary and appended after it, forming an analogue of a residual connection along the sequence dimension. On SummHay, REMORY improves source attribution at nearly unchanged insight coverage and approaches the full-context joint score using only 5.2% of the input positions. Across long-horizon agent benchmarks, Qwen3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash show consistent gains with residual memory. Both models also exhibit substantially fewer repeated tool outputs and tool errors on BrowseComp and Terminal-Bench 2.1.

entries.name: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
entries.purpose: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.

entries.name: UltraText Bench: A Comprehensive Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Text Rendering in Image Generation
entries.purpose: Dense visual text requires image generators to reproduce long strings across multiple regions with correct placement and legibility. As short-string rendering improves, evaluation must test sustained performance across more demanding scenes. We introduce UltraText Bench, a bilingual benchmark for prompt-only generation of dense visual text. It contains 432 prompts spanning 24 real-world scene categories and three difficulty levels, split equally between English and Chinese. Each human-reviewed prompt supplies exact strings for four to twelve text regions, paired with structured references for their content, placement, and visual attributes. We use the Q-Judger vision-language model to assess each image against the complete reference, reporting text fidelity, text clarity, spatial quality, and scene quality. Across 24 model configurations, these dimensions reveal different strengths: Z-Image-Turbo gains 3.81 clarity points over Z-Image-Base while losing 14.76 fidelity points under the reported settings. Performance also varies with workload; Qwen-Image-2512's English composite falls from 86.50 at L1 to 42.86 at L3. Ten participants took part in human evaluation of the automatic scores. Repository: https://github.com/LINs-lab/UltraText_Bench.

entries.name: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling
entries.purpose: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.

entries.name: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code
entries.purpose: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.

entries.name: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
entries.purpose: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.

entries.caveat: Environment image, timeout and permitted commands change results independently of the model. Version and harness both matter: 2.0 and 2.1 are different instruments, and cards report Terminus, Claude Code and Codex harness numbers for the same version. Frontier-Bench is this series' next version rather than a separate benchmark: frontierbench.ai now bills it as "Terminal-Bench 3.0 (formerly Frontier-Bench)", built by the makers of Harbor and Terminal-Bench, so its mentions are counted here. Merging it did not raise this count: all three cards that named Frontier-Bench (Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5, Kimi K3) also report Terminal-Bench in the same document, and the counting unit is the document, so each still adds one. Being a new version, its task set is not comparable to a 2.x number. Not to be confused with Cognition's FrontierCode, a separate instrument recorded separately despite the shared prefix.

entries.name: KORBench

entries.caveat: Long-tail professional forum-based benchmark; evaluates complex reasoning across 20 academic and industrial fields with authentic professional scenarios.
entries.name: LPFQA

entries.caveat: Open-source agent benchmark from Harvey (github.com/harveyai/harvey- labs): 1,200+ tasks across 24 practice areas, all-pass LLM-judge grading. Absolute scores are very low across all models (0-13%), so ordering at the top is decided by a handful of tasks and small gaps are noise.
entries.name: Legal Agent Benchmark

entries.caveat: Contents change by release date; each date is a different benchmark.
entries.name: LiveBench

entries.caveat: Reported as an Elo rating against competitive-programming problems, not a pass rate, so it cannot be read on the same axis as LiveCodeBench.
entries.name: LiveCodeBench Pro

entries.caveat: Multi-turn dialogue benchmark built from sports commentary; evaluates ultra multi-turn, cross-turn, and interactive multi-turn capabilities.
entries.name: MARS-Bench

entries.caveat: Video understanding benchmark. For non-video-native models, uses 1 fps frame extraction. Scores depend on frame sampling strategy and context length.
entries.name: MMVU

entries.caveat: Translation from a single grammar book, reported as half-book and full-book variants that are not interchangeable.
entries.name: MTOB

entries.caveat: Video understanding benchmark. For non-video-native models, uses 1 fps frame extraction. Scores depend on frame sampling strategy and context length.
entries.name: MVbench

entries.caveat: Multilingual SWE-bench variant spanning 7 programming languages; cross-repository context transfer is the measured capability.
entries.name: Multi-SWE-Bench

entries.caveat: Multi-turn instruction retention, graded by an LLM judge.
entries.name: MultiChallenge

entries.caveat: Multi-turn instruction retention, graded by an LLM judge.
entries.name: MultiChallenge

entries.caveat: Long-context recall and use; a "with tools" figure is not comparable to a no-tools run.
entries.name: OneMillionBench

entries.caveat: Physics problem-solving benchmark; multi-step reasoning quality affects the final answer.
entries.name: PhyBench

entries.caveat: Security engineering benchmark; evaluates both vulnerability detection and secure coding practices.
entries.name: SEC-Bench Pro

entries.caveat: Multimodal chemical reasoning; image and formula parsing quality moves the reported figure.
entries.name: SUPERChem

entries.caveat: Reports three splits (Codebase Q&A, Test Writing, Refactoring) as separate figures; the split is part of the instrument.
entries.name: SWE Atlas

entries.caveat: Software engineering freelancer tasks from Upwork; real-world constraints and client communication are part of the task.
entries.name: SWE-Lancer

entries.caveat: Ultra long-horizon software engineering tasks; the score depends on the agent's loop budget as much as on coding skill.
entries.name: SWE-Marathon

entries.caveat: Measures secure-coding behaviour, not exploitation capability.
entries.name: SecCodeBench

entries.caveat: Measures whether curated Agent Skills raise agent pass rates, not raw model capability; the meaningful figure is the paired no-Skills versus curated-Skills gap. The release date follows the paper's first submission.
entries.name: SkillsBench

entries.caveat: End-to-end vibe-coding benchmark by authors at Replit and Georgian AI Lab, scoring web applications from the user's perspective. Tasks are derived from anonymized Replit production traces, so the benchmark is first-party to one of the agents it measures. It reaches this registry through a customer testimonial in Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 / Mythos 5 launch post, where it is described qualitatively and never scored in the comparison table. Distinct from VBench, an unrelated video-generation benchmark.
entries.name: ViBench

entries.caveat: Large-scale file-workspace tasks; the environment and file dependencies are part of the measurement.
entries.name: WorkspaceBench

entries.caveat: First benchmark that jointly evaluates general intelligence, innovation, and autonomous execution, via 60 project-level scientific research tasks spanning 11 domains, progressively withdrawing human guidance. Very new (arXiv 2608.17271, code at github.com/apexin-ai/ASI-Bench) and intended to probe superintelligence-level behaviour, so high variance across seeds and scaffolds should be expected before any vendor adopts it. Only the seed-31415 instances are public; the seed-42 references stay private for official leaderboard scoring, so a locally computed score and a leaderboard score are not the same measurement. This registry's maintainer is one of the benchmark's authors.
entries.name: ASI-Bench

entries.caveat: Four synthetic abductive-reasoning datasets (Animal and Person domains, each Simple and Confounded): the model must supply the missing fact that explains an observation. The paper itself reports that fine-tuned models partly learned to exploit the structure of the data, so a high fine-tuned score need not mean general abduction, and a number without the subset named is not comparable across reports.
entries.name: AbductionRules

entries.caveat: A promptable evaluation framework rather than a fixed test set: it plans its own queries per model, so two runs need not ask the same questions. It does report numbers -- an average score per round and the per-prompt scores behind it -- but each is measured over the handful of prompts that run chose for that model, so they describe the run rather than a scale models can be ranked on.
entries.name: Evaluation Agent

entries.caveat: Pass-rate results are model-scaffold measurements over the 97 released tasks with one trajectory per system-task pair, so a reported percentage is not a model-only number and does not estimate reliability beyond this release or under a different scaffold.
entries.name: FrontierChallenge

entries.caveat: About 32.2K general-science claims, balanced across Supported, Refuted and Not-Enough-Info, generated automatically from SciQ crowd-sourced exam questions by the Multi2Claim pipeline (EACL 2023). Annotators judged a quarter of claims answerable without the evidence, so part of a score can come from world knowledge rather than verification. Only 50 examples are public; the full set is on request.
entries.name: Gsci-Fact

entries.caveat: An ICLR 2026 poster on joint audio-visual reasoning in Omni-LLMs, built with strict audio-video correlation across five cognitive dimensions and four audio information types. Because the question set requires both modalities, vendors that only report vision-only or audio-only figures are not comparable on this instrument. Automated annotation pipeline; manual verification effort is not quantified.
entries.name: JointAVBench

aliases: Large Language Models Are Not Strong Abstract Reasoners
LLMs Are Not Strong Abstract Reasoners
entries.caveat: A suite of abstract-reasoning tasks (IJCAI 2024), several of them text encodings of visual puzzles such as ARC, ACRE and RAVEN, plus PVR and tasks drawn from OpenAI Evals. A text-encoded ARC score is not comparable with a visual ARC score, and the source puzzles are public, so contamination cannot be ruled out.
entries.name: LLM Abstract Reasoning Benchmark

entries.caveat: A robustness variant of LogiQA with the same three subsets as ReClor-plus (shuffled options, correct choice replaced by "none of the other options is correct", and both). A score is only meaningful next to the original LogiQA score and with the subset named, and the source questions are public.
entries.name: LogiQA-plus

entries.caveat: A robustness variant of LogiQA 2.0 with the same three subsets as ReClor-plus. As with its siblings, the drop from the original LogiQA 2.0 score is the measurement, a single blended number hides which variation caused it, and the source questions are public.
entries.name: LogiQAv2-plus

entries.caveat: Track 2 of the MER2026 challenge: open-vocabulary, fine-grained emotion recognition from video, audio and subtitles, ranked on a 1,000-sample test set with emotion-wheel-based metrics that group synonyms (happy and joyful count as one label). Because the label space is open, how a system normalizes its vocabulary onto the wheel moves the score independently of recognition. Reference labels were built by merging top MER2025 team predictions and then manually validated.
entries.name: MER2026 MER-FG

entries.caveat: 150K medical claims (50K each Supported, Refuted, Not-Enough-Info) generated automatically from MedMCQA exam questions by the Multi2Claim pipeline (EACL 2023), not written by fact-checkers. Labels come from the generator, with sampled annotator agreement rather than full review. Only 50 examples are public; the full set is available from the authors on request.
entries.name: Med-Fact

entries.caveat: Solver-certified normal logic programs verbalized into natural language, each labelled under four negation semantics (SLDNF, well-founded, and credulous and skeptical stable-model reasoning) that can disagree on the same instance. A score without the semantics named is not comparable. Models are also sensitive to rule order. The leaderboard's hidden test split (Hugging Face qbao775/naf-bench, as described by the repository README at revision 83ede91) has 495 rows drawn from only 77 programs, so the effective sample is the program, not the row. The arXiv v1 appendix describes an earlier 385-prompt evaluation set over 77 programs, so a paper number and a leaderboard number are not on the same split.
entries.name: NAFBench

entries.caveat: 1,000 audio-visual reasoning questions over 628 videos (seconds to 30 minutes long), targeting synergistic audio-visual understanding in Omni MLLMs, by the NJU-LINK team; an ICLR 2026 poster. Video length and audio-video correlation vary widely, so per-model results depend heavily on which subset is sampled and on frame/audio chunking strategy.
entries.name: OmniVideoBench

entries.caveat: Synthetic multi-step deductive reasoning over natural-language facts and rules under a closed-world assumption, with about 100,000 examples at each reasoning depth from 2 to 5 (nearly 400,000 in total) over animal and people entities. An aggregate number hides the per-depth breakdown the dataset was built to expose, and a model fine-tuned on the templated training split is not comparable with one prompted zero-shot.
entries.name: PARARULE-Plus

entries.caveat: Announced by Scale AI on 2026-08-07 and still in preview: it is soliciting task contributions rather than reporting results, so no model card in this registry reports it and its adoption count is zero. That zero is a real reading, not a gap in the crawl. Recorded now so the benchmark is addressable by name before any score exists, and so the first card to report it has an id to resolve against. Scores are per-task against a baseline under a fixed compute budget, graded on reliability, efficiency, generality and idea quality, so a single headline number should not be expected. Not to be confused with the llm-stats "RSI Index" record, which is a different instrument.
entries.name: RSI-Bench

entries.caveat: A robustness variant of ReClor in three subsets: shuffled options, the correct choice replaced by "none of the other options is correct", and both combined. Read it against the same model's score on the original ReClor, because the gap is the signal; one blended number hides which variation caused the drop, and the source questions are public.
entries.name: ReClor-plus

entries.caveat: Repository-level scientific software engineering benchmark from the OpenMOSS team (Fudan): 119 tasks across 98 GitHub repositories in 20 scientific domains, organized into Issue-driven, Expert-exploratory, and Engineering-integration paradigms. Best reported pass@1 is below 50% (Claude Code with Opus-5 max), and the paper identifies four recurring failure mechanisms, so scores are highly sensitive to scientific-domain knowledge and tool access, not only to coding ability.
entries.name: SWE-bench Science

entries.caveat: 1,664 claims from 180 papers in machine learning, NLP and medicine, verified against tables and figures. Refuted cases keep the authentic claim and edit the evidence instead, so a refuted item can differ from a supported one only in a small change to a table or figure. The authors report that figure-based verification remains particularly challenging for all models, so a blended score depends on the table/figure mix, and table and figure numbers are not interchangeable.
entries.name: SciClaimEval

entries.caveat: Eight tasks that couple understanding and generation, each scored on a text channel and an image channel. One headline number hides which channel earned it, and a model that only understands or only generates is structurally capped on tasks that require both.
entries.name: Uni-MMMU

entries.caveat: Sixteen dimensions folded into a Quality Score and a Semantic Score and then into one Total Score. Every dimension is min-max normalized across the models on the leaderboard at the time, so a total states a model's standing within that pool rather than an absolute rate, and two totals read from different leaderboard revisions are not the same measurement.
entries.name: VBench

entries.caveat: Extends VBench to image-to-video generation and adds trustworthiness dimensions, so its totals are computed over a different dimension set. A VBench++ number is not a VBench number for the same model.
entries.name: VBench++

entries.caveat: Targets intrinsic faithfulness -- physics, commonsense and anatomy -- rather than the surface quality VBench 1.x measures, and is built to stay unsaturated where that suite tops out. Low scores here do not contradict high VBench scores; the two suites ask different questions.
entries.name: VBench-2.0

model_card_leaderboard.measures: When an AI lab releases a model, it publishes a report listing the tests it ran. This counts how many of those reports mention each test. A test near the top is one almost everyone runs, which is not the same as a good one: labs keep running a popular test out of habit, even after the scores stop telling anyone much.

reported_benchmarks.caveat: Published by Zapier over its own automation surface, and cards report different task subsets of it.
reported_benchmarks.name: AutomationBench

reported_benchmarks.caveat: Environment image, timeout and permitted commands change results independently of the model. Version and harness both matter: 2.0 and 2.1 are different instruments, and cards report Terminus, Claude Code and Codex harness numbers for the same version. Frontier-Bench is this series' next version rather than a separate benchmark: frontierbench.ai now bills it as "Terminal-Bench 3.0 (formerly Frontier-Bench)", built by the makers of Harbor and Terminal-Bench, so its mentions are counted here. Merging it did not raise this count: all three cards that named Frontier-Bench (Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5, Kimi K3) also report Terminal-Bench in the same document, and the counting unit is the document, so each still adds one. Being a new version, its task set is not comparable to a 2.x number. Not to be confused with Cognition's FrontierCode, a separate instrument recorded separately despite the shared prefix.
reported_benchmarks.name: Terminal-Bench

reported_benchmarks.caveat: An Elo estimate against human contestants, not a fixed dataset. The problem set moves continuously and rating conversion differs by vendor.
reported_benchmarks.name: Codeforces

reported_benchmarks.caveat: Cleanroom program-rebuild tasks; most models score low, so small differences sit within run-to-run noise.
reported_benchmarks.name: ProgramBench

reported_benchmarks.caveat: Multi-step agentic benchmark using Claude Code harness. Tool Search disabled. Scores depend on harness, reasoning effort, context length, and timeout settings.
reported_benchmarks.name: Agents' Last Exam

reported_benchmarks.name: NL2Repo

The task set was revised after an answer-key audit, so the item count moved and scores are not comparable across dataset versions.

limits: This is triage for a reader deciding what to open next. It is not peer review, a quality verdict, or an endorsement.
Relevance reads only the title and source-published description. Nothing this project writes about a record can earn it points.
Negative signals demote only named artifact patterns. Result indexes, submission placeholders, and visualization-only companions are suppressed; the selection funnel reports how many were removed.
Adoption measures attention, not correctness. Counters that accumulate without a human decision (downloads, likes) are capped below the top of the adoption scale; stars and citations are not.
This project's own repository (ktwu01/benchmark-radar) is excluded from its own ranking.
Attention observations are shown separately and are never quality-scored.
Watchlisted artifacts are retained whatever they score and sort first. Their rank reflects that request, not a higher score.
Update-driven recency is discounted from first announcements using the source's event kind. This cannot distinguish a material GitHub release from a packaging bump.
Structural checks use only missing or populated record fields as a provenance signal. They do not judge benchmark quality, novelty, or validity.
